events.title: JavaScript name announced by Netscape and Sun
events.summary: Netscape and Sun issued a joint press release naming LiveScript as JavaScript and positioning it beside Java.
events.about: This was the public naming of the browser scripting language — not Java itself. JavaScript stayed on the page for UI logic; Java applets handled heavier embedded apps. The name caused decades of confusion, but the split stuck: JS for the web document, Java for compiled JVM programs.

narrative.whyChosen: The naming and marketing moment locked JavaScript into the open web platform story.
narrative.whyImportant: 28 vendors endorsed it as an open scripting standard path toward ECMAScript.
narrative.problemSolved: The web needed a standard, embeddable scripting layer that page authors could use without compiling.

events.title: Ruby 0.95 publicly released
events.summary: Yukihiro Matsumoto published Ruby 0.95 to Japanese newsgroups — the first public release of the language.
events.about: Ruby is an expressive object-oriented scripting language — everything is an object, blocks are first-class. Used for web apps (especially via Rails), DevOps tools (Chef, Vagrant), and quick scripts. Matz optimized for developer happiness over raw performance.

narrative.whyChosen: Ruby prioritized developer happiness and later became the host language for Rails.
narrative.whyImportant: Everything-is-an-object and blocks influenced later languages like Swift and Elixir.
narrative.problemSolved: Matz wanted a true OO scripting language more elegant than Perl and more practical than Python for his taste.
